body:
The application should prevent JNDI injection attacks by properly validating and sanitizing user input before using it in a JNDI query. (We have items for SQL injection, LDAP injection, SMTP injection,... but we don't have an item for JNDI injection)

Rationale:

JNDI injection is a type of attack that occurs when an attacker is able to inject malicious data into the JNDI data source used by an application, allowing them to execute arbitrary code on the application server. Proper validation and sanitization of user input can prevent this type of attack by ensuring that only safe data is used in JNDI queries.

Remediation:

Validate user input by checking that it conforms to the expected format, length, and range of values.
Use parameterized JNDI queries to prevent malicious data from being interpreted as part of the query.
Sanitize user input by removing or encoding special characters that could be used to inject malicious data into the JNDI query.
Review and test the application's input validation and sanitization mechanisms to ensure they are properly implemented and effective.

Testing Method:

- Verify that the application properly validates and sanitizes the input before using it in the JNDI query.


References:

[Exploiting JNDI Injections](https://www.veracode.com/blog/research/exploiting-jndi-injections-java)

From ChatGTP: 

In the case of JNDI injection, the issue is not about safely including data in another context; it's about the unsafe invocation of a method (InitialContext.lookup() in this case) with untrusted data. Therefore, the primary defenses against JNDI injection are:

Input Validation: Whitelist the allowable JNDI references.
Least Privilege: Limit what the JNDI context can do.
Patch and Update: Keep your libraries and runtime up-to-date.
Why Encoding Doesn't Fit Here
Encoding is about taking data that could be interpreted in multiple ways and making sure it's interpreted in only one way. For example, you might encode < as < in HTML to make sure it's interpreted as a text character and not as the start of an HTML tag. But in the case of JNDI injection, the problem isn't multiple interpretations; it's that the single interpretation (as a JNDI reference) is potentially dangerous.

A More Technical Dive
Let's get more technical for a moment. The InitialContext.lookup() method expects a String that represents a valid JNDI name. Encoding this String would not prevent it from being a valid JNDI name; it would just make it a different JNDI name. For instance, if you URL-encode the string, the lookup() method would still perform a lookup; it would just look up a different (encoded) name. This doesn't solve the problem; it just moves it.

The Right Tools for the Job
In security, it's crucial to use the right tool for the job. Encoding is a fantastic tool, but it's not the right one for preventing JNDI injection. For JNDI injection, the tools you want are input validation, least privilege, and patching—these are your hammers, saws, and screwdrivers for this particular job.

So, while encoding is a cornerstone of many security measures, it's not the go-to solution for every type of attack. Always assess the nature of the vulnerability you're dealing with and apply the appropriate mitigations. Keep those tools in your toolbox well-organized!

> Here is an example in Java where validation really is the right defense.
> 
> ![Screenshot 2023-09-26 at 1 02 23 PM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/531465/270782577-8b874225-4dd6-41a5-90fc-af36f1c0edf7.jpg)

So @jmanico I would pendantically argue that input validation is verifying that input received matches the business logic expectations for a particular field whereas sanitization/encoding is either removing, transforming or rejecting data which is dangerous in a particular context. I accept that this particular examples sits on the border of that.

> You can also limit what JNDI can do:
> 
> ```
> Hashtable<String, String> env = new Hashtable<>();
> env.put(Context.INITIAL_CONTEXT_FACTORY, "com.sun.jndi.rmi.registry.RegistryContextFactory");
> env.put(Context.PROVIDER_URL, "rmi://localhost:1099");
> InitialContext context = new InitialContext(env);
> ```
> 
> By setting the INITIAL_CONTEXT_FACTORY and PROVIDER_URL, you're limiting the types of services that the JNDI context can interact with.

I think these are good points and I would modify the requirement to say:

5.2.11 | [ADDED] Verify that the application appropriately sanitizes untrusted input before use in Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI) queries **and that JNDI is configured as securely as possible** to prevent JNDI injection attacks. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓
-- | -- | -- | -- | --

Pattern matching with a RegEx is straight-up validation. This data is NOT being cleaned up (sanitization) or converted (encoded) in any way. If the pattern is not matched, the data is not used.

But I am being pedantic as well. I am happy with your proposed requirement so long as you are not preaching encoding to stop this attack, which would be wrong IMO.

Thanks Jim, I think we are aligned :)

5.2.11 | [ADDED] Verify that the application appropriately sanitizes untrusted input before use in Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI) queries and that JNDI is configured as securely as possible to prevent JNDI injection attacks. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓
